Cure has a very interesting and original premise- that we might be manipulated to commit crimes because of our instincts. I do not quite agree wit what Cure tries to tell us- that everyone has some kind of thoughts to kill, or at least, to make a person disappear from their lives. It is a very dangerous thing to believe, that only society with its rules keeps us from murdering other people- and, as we see in the movie, it does not require a lot of efforts to make someone kill others. The exaggeration of the premise does not work and fit in a crime movie- it is laughable to believe that someone can easily hypnotize us to kill. The fact that, by the end of the film, only a look is required to pass the urge to kill (the main character does not even talk to the waitress and she is already manipulated to commit a crime- by using her knife) is far-fetched and, I would say, disturbing for disturbing's sake.

Tarantino is the kind of director who can take on any genre in the world and make an award winning film out of it. Though a western film, Django isn't a cowboy hero, rather a free slave anti-hero. He's neither good nor bad, but is a steadfast individual who ends up learning a whole lot from the German bounty hunter who freed him. The only thing he wants back is his beloved wife, but ends up facing brutal violence, harsh negotiating, and formidable plantation owners. The fiery revenge in Django's attitude throughout the film gives the feeling that he might explode at any given second, yet he somehow fastens it to a leash. He is an attentive, patient, yet zealous man slowly making his way from the bottom to the top. The use of wide angle filming in this movie captures every bit of vivid landscape imaginable in 19th century Texas, giving the viewers a deeper appreciation for Tarantino's masterful filming in which he habitually displays. it's an violent action packed character-driven drama. Really can't say much more than this. Just watch it now.

Comedian turned virtuoso director and Oscar winner Jordan Peele has already proved himself to be a master of the horror genre, expertly interlacing thrills with hard-hitting social commentary to deliver smash hit films like “Get Out (2017)” and “Us (2019)”. The Sixth Sense is a horror-thriller directed by M.Night Shyamalan who proves that, when he wants, he can come up with unique, creative ideas that challenge the idea of being and living. In terms of script, the film is perfect - the way it is structured is a clever one that makes you constantly pay attention to what is happening on screen. I was thinking towards the end of the film, that, even without knowing about the extraordinary and shocking twist, it would still be a flawless film- every character is presented well enough to grow on you while you are waiting for the final revelation. I did not expect it at all, but even without it, The Sixth Sense meant a lot to me- the kid's journey of self-release was slow, but steady, leaving some messages behind- he was not able to talk to living people, they didn't want to listen to him because of their selfish belief that paranormal did not exist: instead he could understand the wishes of the dead ones, who could truly appreciate the nature of living. "I was repeating my lines" said the boy somewhere in the story, even though we were seen that he did not have any- he kept them for the ghosts he would meet, because he started to feel important, useful to them. The film portrays how short and fragile life truly is- and how many regrets we carry with us till our death, and even beyond. The twist isn't the reason why the film is brilliant, it's actually the assurance that we'll be left truly shocked and changed in a way or another after watching it. 5/5
